toc.title: Are we ever done building safety?

sections.title: Reconnect with someone in your life

blocks.h: Are we ever done building safety?

blocks.p: No, I don't think so. In part, because our safety access is always challenged. We constantly need to build its strength in order to tolerate the world around us.

We live in a society with top-down structures, rules, and norms like government, religions, families, workplaces, and cultures. Those top-down structures surely have policies, procedures, and practices you do not agree with or maybe even find reprehensible. Could you exist in complete safety with these structures looming over your head? I doubt it.

We also live in societies with people that have very different and even wildly contrasting values than we do. These individuals range from nuisances to what can only be considered evil. Could you exist in complete safety while sharing spaces with these individuals and not knowing who they are? I doubt that as well.

However, despite this, you have some access to safety. Or enough access to safety. But complete access? No. I don't even know what complete access to safety would be like. Is it happiness? Excitement? Joy? Awe? Peace? Tranquility? Relaxation? Let's abandon that idea of complete safety state activation. That doesn't seem realistic. (And what would happen to us if our sympathetic and dorsal systems were switched off entirely? Doesn't seem good. We need these for basic bodily functions.)

In the place of complete safety state activation, let's put in another idea: growing the capacity of our safety state. Each of us has a present-moment capacity for safety. This capacity depends on numerous factors, such as upbringing, attachment to caregivers, daily stress, etc. Each of us is limited in our safety capacity in some way.

So, the focus should be on growing our safety capacity. Yes, that may mean changing the external world for the better. Better top-down government and other societal structures will impact our capacity for safety, so changing them may allow for more safety in our system. I won't tell you what I think those should be; we all have our idea of what's best.

However, that can't be our sole focus. And for you, it's not. You're reading this, which is all about your ability to access your safety state. This is not about society and not even about co-regulation. It's about you and the building blocks of self-regulation. You already know the importance of your role when it comes to growing your capacity for safety.

I hope your capacity for safety has already grown from reading and applying these ideas. I know they have for me and the members of the Unstucking Academy. I hope that your safety capacity is more tomorrow than it is right now. Don't worry about ever getting complete safety state activation. Instead, focus on growing your safety capacity daily.

As you do, you will notice more distress tolerance. You will notice that things that were previously distressing are less distressing. You'll notice more capacity for connection, curiosity, confidence, and calm in your life.

Not only do I think we're never done building our safety state… I hope we never are! I hope that we always have opportunities for growth and challenge. If we somehow finished strengthening our safety state, what would that mean? Would that mean we no longer face obstacles in life? Would that mean we are complacent and not challenging ourselves? That we have no new connections to make?

I hope that you are challenging yourself in new ways. When you challenge yourself, you lose access to your safety state. At least, you lose a noticeable amount of access. You get anxious when you try something new. You have doubts. You worry. All of this indicates losing at least a bit of safety access. But this also means you can experience distress, successfully navigate the challenge anyway, and re-anchor in safety. This process of challenging and succeeding will continue to grow your vagal brake and distress tolerance.
These new challenges are growth points for us. So, I hope that we're never done increasing the capacity of our safety states. I hope we constantly find new challenges to grow from.
If you are genuinely content with the progress you've made, then you can focus your trauma recovery journey on building safety.

It's entirely okay to continually focus on building the strength of your safety state. Your stuck defensive state may have begun to soften already and will continue to do so as you practice safety. I don't think this process is ever entirely done anyhow, so there is no harm in choosing to focus solely on your daily safety practice.

If you stay focused entirely on safety, you will likely notice more grounding in your daily life. You will likely notice your defensive activation reduces and softens. I don't know if it ever goes away entirely, but things get much easier. However, the underlying stuck defensive state still exists, just with much less intensity. It may still surface in your dreams and daily life, but less often and more tolerably. You'll be better able to approach this activation with compassion, coping skills will be more effective, and safety grounding will be easier. Basically, life gets better all around.

Not only does life get better, but you have more opportunities for growth as you continually focus on your safety state. These growth opportunities will bring challenges, but you'll be better able to handle the defensive activation that comes along with them. Here are some options as you keep building:

Especially through the [A->W->E Method](piece:safety-stacking-awe#a-w-e-method). In this stage, you can continually practice mindfulness, noticing what safety feels like and extending it through Anchored Awareness, Witnessing, and Experiencing. You can also continue to use the various safety Anchoring Potentials you have experimented with already. Focus on the ones that are the most helpful. As you gain confidence in those, try out the more challenging ones again and see if they are more manageable now. Try them inside and outside of your Passive Safety Environment.

Something new that brings you safety experiences. Or something old that you want to make new again. Hobbies are a great way to connect with yourself with a sense of fun or interest. They can be entertaining, like writing a short story. Or they can be fulfilling, like volunteering in your community. But hobbies could also lead you to connect with new people with the same interests, like joining a regular bicycling meetup.

Every day, use micro moments of mindfulness to connect to your environment. These moments help you to stay out of your head and connect to the world around you. Use your senses and identify experiences that bring you safety. Small moments go a long way, especially with a mindful breath or two.

blocks.h3: Reconnect with someone in your life

blocks.p: If you can do so, reconnect with someone in your life. Find someone that feels safe and do so in an approachable way. This person should not be someone who will trigger defensiveness. You may feel some defense activation simply at reconnecting with someone. That's enough for now. Allow that, but connect in a way that feels approachable. Don't add on further defensive activation by trying to connect with someone who cannot receive it or is otherwise overtly triggering.

The person you reconnect with can be someone you interacted with yesterday; it doesn't have to be a friend from childhood. And the connection doesn't have to be a deeply emotional experience; it could be just saying, "Hi." Listen to what you can tolerate and take a step forward. If you can handle more the next day, accept that challenge as you are ready.

If you're ready to create a deeper connection, you can do so through simple means. One option is to express appreciation to someone for who they are or how they have positively impacted you. Send them an impromptu text message and let them know they're on your mind and you appreciate them. Write a heartfelt card for your grandchildren and send it through snail mail. Or send a selfie video to your best friend and give them some love.

If you are not yet ready to reconnect with someone, then focus on new connections. Keep it simple and light, like sharing chit-chat or a smile with a clerk in your favorite store. These opportunities provide small moments of co-regulation.

You could also connect with someone new in places you are already a part of, like your workplace or religious institutions. The goal is not to develop a deep new friendship or love life. The goal is to share small moments of co-regulation without expectations for the future.

These are some options for continuing to practice safety or challenging yourself by going deeper into it. Whether or not you choose to go to the next step, I highly recommend using these practices. A stronger safety state is always needed, and especially before working directly with your stuck defensive state.
I'll nerd you out here and discuss homeostasis. And then I'll share why I am nerding you out.

"Homeostasis" is our body's ability to maintain a stable and balanced internal environment throughout its numerous organs and functions. Homeostasis optimizes using our bodily resources to reach and maintain a balanced internal environment, even as the external environment changes. Homeostasis requires a well-regulated autonomic nervous system to function.

When the ANS is well-regulated, this results in more efficiency in heart rate, breathing, digestion, and much more. But to have a well-regulated ANS, the ventral vagal safety state needs to be active. The ventral pathways are key to keeping defensive activation lessened and the heart beating calmer. In other words, ventral vagal activation is at the core of homeostasis. When the body is in its safety state, homeostasis can occur and maintain, utilizing all of the autonomic pathways for the benefit of the body.

If not, then the body uses its resources for defensive activation. Defensive activation is not a bad thing as long as it's initiated and completed in a short time period in response to danger. If not, prolonged activation of defense keeps the body out of homeostatic self-regulation due to the inactive safety state.

Trauma is being stuck in a defensive state. If the body is stuck in trauma, it is not in an ideal homeostatic state. Bodily processes and resources are not optimized for "health, growth, and restoration." Instead, they're used for unending defensive activation. This results in numerous physical, mental, and behavioral problems, as shown through the Adverse Childhood Experiences study.

Of course, the solution to coming out of trauma is to activate the safety state and self-regulate. Once the body is more self-regulated, homeostatic functioning initiates, continues, or improves. The safety state repurposes defensive states for prosocial functions through the mixed states (intimacy, stillness, and play).
"Okay, Justin! Okay! But why are you telling me this?" you desperately ask.
"Because your body is compelled to self-regulate. Your body is compelled toward homeostasis," I reply.

Our bodies function better when they are in homeostatic self-regulation. If there were an ideal way of being, this would be it. When in homeostasis and self-regulation, our bodies simply do better. Our cognitions do. Our behaviors. Our relationships. Everything just gets better.

Think of us as organisms just like any other. We are biological processes that must use resources ideally to function better. Our bodies, simply as living things, gravitate toward self-regulation, toward homeostasis.
"You're not really answering my question, Justin. Get on with it!" you may be saying.
"Really? Okay, I'll try again," I respond, as I look down and furrow my brow in deep thought.

Our bodies must self-regulate. At every moment of every day, they are attempting to self-regulate. Even right now, your body wants to self-regulate. Why? Because that is its ideal state of being: self-regulation and homeostasis. Self-regulation is not a choice we make. It's a bodily compulsion. Our natural tendency is to self-regulate.
So, we need to get out of the way and allow self-regulation to happen.

Your body wants to. But your conscious mind may not want to. Your stuck state may not want to. Your families, culture, and society may not want you to. But your natural self-regulatory capacity wants to.

As you develop the strength of your safety state, your body's natural self-regulatory capacity will open up. Self-regulation might result in discomfort as defensive activation comes to the forefront of your conscious experience. If this defensive activation is too much, it's time to continue focusing on safety cues and anchors or perhaps to use a coping skill.

But as you anchor into your safety state further, you may notice something else happen. If your safety state is strong and anchored well enough, you may notice an impulse to feel more deeply into yourself, even in your stuck defensive state. I call this the "interest impulse." It's something that my clients, community members, and I have felt: wanting to know more, to feel more. It comes from genuine curiosity and interest, from welcoming and compassion. It does not come from desperation and an attempt to rid the body of a virus called "trauma."
I conceptualize this interest impulse as the conscious experience of the ANS's impulse to self-regulate and initiate ideal homeostatic functioning.

blocks.prompt: Have you noticed an interest impulse: a curious, compassionate pull to know more about what you feel inside?

blocks.p: As you follow the impulse, it will take you inward. You will allow, witness, and experience your stuck defensive state. As you directly experience your defensive activation with compassion and curiosity, the next level of self-regulation can begin. The next level is climbing the Polyvagal ladder out of defense.

Building your safety state is great. A lot of good can come from that. But that doesn't mean the stuck state resolves. It may still be within you. That's the first level of self-regulation. The second level is allowing defense through Anchored Awareness, Witnessing, and Experiencing (A->W->E), resulting in self-regulation. For now, I want you to understand where you are and what you can handle clearly.

If you are feeling the interest impulse, that's a good sign that you're ready to [begin unstucking your defensive state](piece:unstucking-methods). If you truly want to know what your inner world is like, including the defensive and traumatized states, from compassion and curiosity, then you may be ready.

If you are struggling with accessing and maintaining your safety state, you probably need more time and should focus more on building safety. If you feel fear while accessing safety, you should probably stay with safety for now.
